lines: Custom software and web design for the Mississippi Gulf Coast.

slides: Your website has one job. Most don't do it.
A stranger lands on your site with a question. Can I book? Are you open? Do y'all do this?
The site's only job: answer it — then point to the next step.
Call. Book. Order. Walk in. Pick one.
Restaurant → the menu on the page, and "Order" before anyone scrolls.
Salon, studio, clinic → "Book" in the first screen, on your own site.
Shop, bar, venue → hours, address, and a tappable phone number at the top.
The five-second test: hand your phone to a stranger. Ask them what to do.
Decide what you want them to do. Build the page so it's the easiest thing on it. That's design as strategy.
@C-BRAND
Five quiet ways your website loses customers. (Nobody complains. They just leave.)
1 — The menu is a PDF. Pinch, zoom, give up. Google can't read it either.
Fix: a menu that lives on the page. Updates in minutes. Searchable.
2 — Hours on the site don't match hours on Google. Someone's showing up to a locked door.
3 — "Book now" sends people to someone else's site. Now they own the relationship.
4 — The phone number isn't a button. Ten-minute fix.
5 — "Welcome to our website!" is not an action. Call. Book. Order. Walk in. Pick one.
None of this needs a redesign. It needs a decision and an afternoon. Save this.
Six weeks. Two sold-out nights. One phone and one TV.
A ticketing site the owners change themselves. New night, new venue, new price — no code.
A live event app: the host's phone and the venue TV, paired by a five-character code.
Bar wifi is bad. The app caches locally, so the game keeps going when the signal doesn't.
Working link from day one. Live on day 13. Version one in six weeks. First two nights sold out.
@C-BRAND
How a website gets built here. Four steps, no fog.
1. Discovery. A real conversation, no intake forms.
It ends with a scope you can actually read. Sometimes it ends with "you don't need a new site yet." Also fine.
2. Build. A working link from day one — not a mockup reveal at the end.
Change your mind in week one, when changing your mind is cheap.
3. Launch. Tested on real phones. Shipped with a plain-English owner's manual.
4. Care. Fast, secure, current — and grown as the business grows past it.
Same hands, all four steps. Birch Design Lab. Mississippi Gulf Coast. Link in bio.
Three lines every local business homepage needs. (Before anyone scrolls.)
Line 1 — What you are, and where. "Wood-fired pizza in Ocean Springs."
Line 2 — One true, specific reason to choose you. Specific is believable. Vague is invisible.
Line 3 — What to do next. One button: call, book, order, directions.
Not this: "Welcome to our website! We are committed to quality and service." Three lines that say nothing.
This: "Same-day phone repair in Gulfport. The owner fixes it while you wait." Then one button: Call.
@C-BRAND
A design lab, not an agency. What that actually means.
An agency has layers. Your question travels through all of them.
A lab is one bench. The same hands that build your site answer your email.
Working link from day one. No mockup reveal.
Every project ships with a plain-English owner's manual.
Two things, done properly. We say no to the rest.
The job: make what's already good about your business easy to see. Birch Design Lab — link in bio.
